_comment: Guided tour for the decay-analysis shell. Steps are the numbered panels in the left navigation list ('panel' targets) and wait for the user to select the row. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What a decay is, and what it costs to get wrong
steps.text:
A TCSPC decay is a histogram of how long each photon waited after its excitation pulse. Fitting it gives fluorescence lifetimes — and lifetimes are what turn FRET into a distance rather than a ratio of intensities.

The left list is the five tools that produce and calibrate them, in the order they depend on each other. Seven steps.

steps.title: The instrument response comes first
steps.text:
What you measured is not your molecule's decay. It is your molecule's decay convolved with the response of the detector and electronics to an infinitely short flash.

Below about a nanosecond, most of what you are fitting is the IRF. That is why a wrong one is so dangerous: it does not give you a bad fit, it gives you a good fit to the wrong lifetime.

await.hint: Select 1. IRF Estimation on the left.

steps.title: Let the data say how many lifetimes there are
steps.text:
A multi-exponential fit needs the number of components declared before you fit, and that choice usually decides the answer. Two exponentials will describe a broad distribution; three will describe it slightly better.

Maximum entropy returns a distribution instead, so the data can say whether it has one peak or three. Use it to decide the model, then fit.

steps.title: The same fit, over many files
steps.text: Once the settings are right for one file, this runs them across the rest without re-deciding anything. The value is not only the time saved — it is that every file in a series gets identically treated, which is what makes the differences between them interpretable.

steps.title: Starting from raw photons instead
steps.text:
If you have a TTTR stream rather than a binned decay, this is the step before everything above: it builds the micro-time histogram the fits consume.

The choice that matters here is the binning. Too coarse and you smooth away the rise the IRF defines; too fine and every channel is noise.

steps.title: Anisotropy needs its detectors calibrated
steps.text:
An anisotropy is a ratio of two polarization channels, so any difference in their detection efficiency goes straight into it. G is that ratio, measured.

Without it an anisotropy is an instrument reading — and unlike a lifetime, there is nothing in the fit that looks wrong when G is missing.

steps.title: Four checks before you believe a lifetime
steps.text:
1. Look at the weighted residuals, not χ². A χ² near 1 with structure in the residuals means the model is wrong in a way the single number hid.
2. Refit from different starting values. Multi-exponential minima are shallow and correlated; a component that wanders is not determined.
3. Does MEM agree? It got there without being told how many components to expect.
4. Watch the scatter. Excitation light arrives with the IRF and is indistinguishable from a very short lifetime.

The ? button has the long version.
